# Arne Furumark

**Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark** (September 26, 1903 – October 8, 1982) was a Swedish archaeologist and classical scholar specializing in the Aegean Bronze Age. He served as a professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at Uppsala University and as the director of the Swedish Institute at Athens. Furumark is best known for his establishment of the morphological and stylistic classification system for Mycenaean pottery, which became the standard framework for dating and analyzing Late Bronze Age ceramics in the Mediterranean . He also directed excavations at Sinda in Cyprus and San Giovenale in Italy .

## Early life and education
Furumark was born in Kristiania (now Oslo), Norway, on September 26, 1903 . His father was a businessman in the paper industry. Furumark's early life involved work in his father's offices in Oslo and London. During a stay in London at the age of nineteen, he visited the British Museum, an event he later cited as the catalyst for his decision to pursue archaeology rather than a business career .

He enrolled at Uppsala University in Sweden in 1925 to study the humanities. There, he became a student of Axel W. Persson, a prominent archaeologist known for his work on Mycenaean sites . Furumark participated in excavations in Greece under Persson's supervision. He completed his doctoral dissertation, *Studies in Aegean Decorative Art: Antecedent and Sources of the Mycenaean Ceramic Decoration*, at Uppsala University in 1939 . That same year, he was appointed as an associate professor at the university .

## Academic career
Furumark spent the majority of his academic career at Uppsala University. He was appointed Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History in 1952, a position he held until his retirement in 1970 . During his tenure, he supervised several students who later became notable scholars in the field, including Gisela Walberg and Carl Nylander .

In addition to his professorship, Furumark served as the director of the Swedish Institute at Athens from 1956 to 1957 . He was also elected a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1958 .

## Classification of Mycenaean pottery
Furumark's most significant contribution to the field of classical archaeology was his comprehensive systematization of Mycenaean ceramics. In 1941, he published his two-volume magnum opus: *The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification* and *The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery* .

Prior to Furumark's work, the study of Mycenaean pottery relied heavily on the earlier classifications by Adolf Furtwängler and Georg Loeschcke (1886) and the systems devised by Arthur Evans for Minoan Crete . Furumark's work provided the first exhaustive typology for the mainland Greek material. He analyzed the ceramics based on two primary criteria:
* **Shape:** He identified and numbered specific vessel forms, creating a catalog of "Furumark Shapes" (FS) .
* **Decoration:** He cataloged decorative patterns, assigning them "Furumark Motif" (FM) numbers .

This system allowed for a more precise relative chronology of the Late Helladic period. Furumark divided the pottery into stylistic phases, establishing a sequence that demonstrated the continuity of Mycenaean ceramic traditions and their distinction from Minoan styles . His analysis challenged the prevailing view held by Arthur Evans that Mycenaean culture was merely a subordinate offshoot of Minoan civilization, demonstrating instead that mainland pottery had its own independent development while exchanging influences with Crete .

The "Furumark" numbers (e.g., FS 1–333) remain a standard international reference for describing Mycenaean and Minoan pottery . While subsequent scholars, such as Elizabeth French and Penelope Mountjoy, have refined the chronology and incorporated new findings from stratified deposits, Furumark's typology remains the foundational framework for the discipline .

## Archaeological fieldwork

### Sinda, Cyprus
Between 1947 and 1948, Furumark directed excavations at the site of Sinda in the Famagusta district of Cyprus . This project marked the resumption of Swedish archaeological activity on the island following World War II . Furumark selected the site after illicit digging revealed Mycenaean IIIC1b sherds, a type of pottery previously undocumented on Cyprus .

The excavations uncovered a fortified town dating to the Late Bronze Age. Furumark identified three distinct occupation phases:
* **Sinda I:** A town with a defense system, ending in destruction.
* **Sinda II:** A reconstruction featuring Mycenaean IIIC1a and locally produced IIIC1b pottery, also ending in destruction.
* **Sinda III:** A poorer reoccupation characterized by "Close Style" pottery, eventually abandoned .

Furumark originally attributed the destruction of Sinda I to Greek settlers (c. 1230 BC) and the destruction of Sinda II to the Sea Peoples (c. 1190 BC) . However, these interpretations and the associated chronology were later challenged. Paul Åström, who contributed to the final publication of the Sinda excavations in 2003, proposed a lowered chronology and suggested that the destructions might have been caused by pirates or internal conflicts rather than the specific migration waves Furumark hypothesized .

### San Giovenale, Italy
From 1962 to 1963, Furumark conducted excavations at San Giovenale, an Etruscan site in Italy . These excavations were part of a larger project initiated by the Swedish Institute in Rome in the 1950s. Furumark's work focused on the "Borgo" area of the site .

## Other research
### Linear B
Furumark was involved in the early discussions regarding the decipherment of Linear B, the syllabic script used for writing Mycenaean Greek. Although he was initially skeptical of the theory that Linear B represented the Greek language, he corresponded with Michael Ventris, the architect who deciphered the script . Following Ventris's breakthrough in 1952, Furumark was among the first archaeologists to accept the decipherment and apply it to his work . His correspondence from the 1950s includes letters from prominent philologists and archaeologists such as John Chadwick and Massimo Pallottino regarding the script .

### Italian Prehistory
In 1947, Furumark published *Det äldsta Italien* (*The Oldest Italy*), a handbook on Italian prehistory . While intended for a Swedish audience, the work incorporated his research into the archaeological connections between the Aegean and Italy during the Bronze Age .

## Selected bibliography
* Furumark, Arne (1939). *Studies in Aegean Decorative Art: Antecedent and Sources of the Mycenaean Ceramic Decoration*. Uppsala: Uppsala University.
* Furumark, Arne (1941). *The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification*. Stockholm: Kungl. Vitterhets, historie och antikvitets akademien.
* Furumark, Arne (1941). *The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery*. Stockholm: Kungl. Vitterhets, historie och antikvitets akademien.
* Furumark, Arne (1947). *Det äldsta Italien*. Uppsala: Lindblad.
* Furumark, Arne (1950). "The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550-1400 B.C." *Opuscula Archaeologica*, Vol. 6, pp. 150–271.
* Furumark, Arne; Adelman, Charles M. (2003). *Swedish Excavations at Sinda, Cyprus: Excavations Conducted by Arne Furumark 1947–1948*. Stockholm: Paul Åströms Förlag (Posthumous publication).

Description
-----------

When Arne Furumark was entrusted with writing the Late Bronze Age summary volume for the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, he realized that a habitation site was needed in order to clarify problems associated with the last phases of that period. As neither the French nor the Cypriote excavations at Enkomi had yet been published he decided to find his own site: he scouted several, but settled on Sinda because recent illicit digging there had thrown up sherds of a sort never before seen on the Island, namely Mycenaean IIIC1b. He conducted two short excavation seasons but the control excavation he planned was aborted when he received notice from the Cypriote authorities that there was large scale destruction of the site. Although there is evidence of earlier and later habitation at Sinda, the most important is the Late Bronze Age fortified town (probably built along the copper trading route), with its three phases: Sinda I, II, and III.  
Sinda I, which saw the building of the defense system and had a material culture including local Cypriote wares as well as examples of Mycenaean IIIB, suffered major destruction. Sinda II followed: Structures were repaired and built, and were accompanied by a rich material culture including Mycenaean IIIC1a and great quantities of locally produced, early IIIC1b materials. A second catastrophe brought an end to that town. Sinda III followed, a poorer town, but with examples of locally produced, developed IIIC1b wares of the Close Style. Furumark's interpretation that the two destructions were brought about first by Greek settlers and then by Sea Peoples has been challenged by more recent archaeological evidence which lowers the date of Mycenaean IIIB. Paul Astrom, in his summary suggests a reasonable alternative, that pirates and adventurers were responsible for the destructions. -- Provided by publisher

\[The Table of Contents is listed below.\]

The site of San Giovenale was excavated by the Swedish Institute of Classical Studies at Rome between 1956 and 1965. It is in the Comune of Blera, near Viterbo, about 20 km east of Tarquinia and about 27 km north-east of Cerveteri. The ancient city is placed on a tufa mountain comprised of two hills: the western plateau (Acropolis) and the smaller eastern plateau (Borgo).

This volume deals with a small area of the Borgo, the northwest corner where Etruscans built a small metalworking quarter surrounded by defensive walls. The excavation was directed by Carl Nylander with contributions by a large number of people through the years. He is the main author of the volume, together with other scholars.

The “Preface” (pp. 11-12), by Lars Karlsson, gives the geographical framework of the site. San Giovenale is the name of the bishop and saint of Narni to whom a chapel on the Acropolis was dedicated. The ancient name remains unknown. The structure and purposes of the book are clarified by Karlsson in a short summary.

Nylander in “Personal Prolegomena” (21-28) reminisces about the start of the excavation, when he was a young student more interested in Near Eastern archaeology. He introduces all the protagonists of the San Giovenale campaign during those years from a friendly and informal point of view. He speaks about himself using “he” because

> “…the author, at the age of 80 and at the end of his archaeological career, at times feels very much the father of that distant young student and inexperienced excavator of the Borgo, sad and severe at his mistakes, yet not lacking sympathetic understanding and benevolence in view of the young man’s honest and at times quite respectable efforts to handle, according to his limited lights, a rather difficult field situation…”(27).

This intimate view allows consideration of the responsibilities of an archaeologist, in particular his ability to foster knowledge, but also to destroy historical evidence.

Chapter One (29-40) introduces the topography of the Borgo, which was occupied without interruption from the Protovillanovan age to medieval times. The earliest find, a fragment of an early Protocorinthian kotyle (late 8 th century B.C.), and the latest one, a spouted jug (6-7 th century A.D.), testify to the long settlement of the area. This chapter also covers the geology of San Giovenale, whose origin is attributed by Sheldon Judson to the third stage in the development of the landscape. Here, streams began to erode the earlier volcanic deposits, modeling the narrow promontory between the Fammilume river on the north and the Vesca and Pietrisco on the south. A list of building materials at the site follows, offering useful definition of tufa and its variations (“tufo rosso”, “tufo grigio” and “peperino”).

Chapter Two (41-49) covers the history of the Borgo excavation. The site was already mentioned in reports of the years between 1870 and 1880 but the first real excavation took place in 1956 thanks to Erik Wetter and Axel Boëthius of the Swedish Institute in Rome, encouraged by Renato Bartoccini, the Soprintendente of south Etruria, and King Gustaf VI Adolf. Unfortunately no reports about the first two years of the campaign exist. In 1961 research was led by Nylander for four seasons. In 1965 the area was protected by a huge metal roof, called _Capannone_, replaced in 2002. The first report appeared in a 1969 paper by Börje Blomé (“Un inedito insediamento arcaico etrusco in San Giovenale (Viterbo)”, in _Palladio_, 139-154). In this paper he presented the excavation area and a new working method based on the photogrammetric technique, bringing out even then the complexity of the stratigraphy. The project was reactivated in the late 1970s, when a team of scholars began to study the documentation, organizing a symposium (1983) and the exhibition _Architettura etrusca nel viterbese. Ricerche svedesi a San Giovenale e Acquarossa (1956-1986)_. In the following years many scholars participated in the study of the Borgo. This volume contains the examination of the structural remains, while analyses of the pottery can be found in the work published in 2009 by Ingrid Pohl ( _San Giovenale. Vol. V, Fasc.2. The Borgo. The Etruscan habitation quarter on the north-west slope stratification and materials_).

In Chapter Three (50-57) Lars Karlsson offers an overview of the excavation area, phases and stratigraphy. It was possible to establish three pre-house periods (late 8 th -late 7 th c. B.C.) and five building periods (late 7 th B.C.-early 7 th c. A.D.) with an interruption due to a possible earthquake around 550-530 B.C. A general stratigraphy of 11 strata is briefly described together with the most important information about position, composition and finds. All data are organized in a useful table that shows concordances between the different layers and their attribution to a specific period.

Each following chapter analyzes a different developmental phase:

—Pre-House Period I (late 8 th c. to about 675 B.C.) ( Ch. 4 58-66): remains of cuttings in the bedrock to set up a wooden palisade and an oval hut (maybe two?);  
—Pre-House Period II (ca. 675 – late 7 th c. B.C.) ( Ch. 5, 67-71): extension of the palisade and construction of the rectangular House F and an irregular cellar called _Cantina_ G;  
—The Great Fill Project (late 7 th c. B.C.) ( Ch. 6, 72-87): modeling of the landscape (cutting the bedrock, creation of a terrace wall with both defensive and static function, drawing a new drain and three soil levels) for the structures of the following period;  
—The chapters on Period 1 (late 7 th c. – 575 B.C.) and Period 2 (757-530 B.C.) do not follow a chronological order like the previous ones, but are discussed by areas: building of House A in the northern area ( Ch. 7, 88-103), Houses B, whose hypothetic reconstruction was presented in a 2001 work by Börje Blomé (“A tentative reconstruction of House B on the Borgo of San Giovenale”, in _From huts to houses. Transformations of ancient societies_, J. Rasmus Brandt, L. Karlsson (edd.), Stockholm 2001, 241-243), and C in the central area ( Ch. 8, 104-128), Lane K, a sort of alley between Houses B, C and D ( Ch. 9, 129-130), the southern area D/E/F/G ( Ch. 10, 131-137);  
—The earthquake that hit the Borgo between 550 and 530 B.C., dated by the pottery in the fill leveling the floor of the NW area ( Ch. 11, 138-141). This chapter starts with a very interesting introduction to the history of earthquakes in Italy that recalls a previous paper by Börje Blomé and Carl Nylander (“On Etruscan earthquakes and architecture”, in _From huts to houses. Transformations of ancient societies_, J. Rasmus Brandt, L. Karlsson (edd.), Stockholm 2001, 233-239);  
—Period 3, after the earthquake (530-400 B.C.), during which houses were rebuilt and restored. House A testifies to a metallurgical activity ( Ch. 12, 143-147);  
—Periods 4 (4 th – 2 nd c. B.C.) and 5 (medieval) ( Ch. 13, 148-150), see the long, slow abandonment of the area, whose latest phase corresponds to two burials of late 5 th – early 6 th century A.D. ( Ch. 13, 148-150).

The discussion ends with a summary of the periods ( by Karlsson, 151-153). An interesting series of Appendices completes the volume.

The division into chronological phases is a development and a further specialization of the one presented a few years ago by Ingrid Pohl in her 2009 work (see above), where it was composed of 5 main phases (Pre-House strata, c. 800-650? BC; Building Period I, c. 650-530 BC; Building Period II, c. 530-/500-430 BC; Building Period III, c. 430/410 BC; Post-habitation Period, medieval period).

After an extensive bibliography of the archaeological research in San Giovenale (1877-2011) in Appendix 1 (by Kerstin Bellerba and Brita Alroth, 155-159), Appendix 2 ( 161-163) contains a discussion about building techniques, which Barbara Bellelli Marchesini considers as very important experimental phases gradually determining the passage from huts to houses in the Tyrrhenian area. The advanced skills of architects who planned the Borgo are confirmed by the analyses made by Marie Klingspor Rotstein and Daniel Kwiatkowski on the stone walls, which show that mortars were used to join the blocks (165-175). A typology of roof-tiles is discussed by Örjan Wikander, who updates his 1981 study, finding interesting parallels with Acquarossa despite the still limited availability of materials (178-181). The last Appendix (183-189), in both English and Italian, by Angela Bizzarro, clarifies the methods used through the years to document the excavation, from the pencil drawings to the latest digital elaborations.

The main strength of the volume is the accuracy of the documentation. The 160 figures, 43 plates and 2 fold-out plans, comprise photographs, drawings (also old sketches), reconstructions, photographic montages, digitalized plans and sections, and many useful re-elaborated photos. These photos, several of them in color, clarify and make understandable the complexity of the structures.

The reader might miss a general map placing the site within ancient Etruria. However, the specific nature of the topic, devoted to the presentation and interpretation of the architecture, implies a readership of scholars who already know the importance of San Giovenale for the study of Etruscan architecture. This book does not cover the development of the Etruscan house plan, of which the houses of the Borgo and the Acropolis represent a milestones (see Appendix 1 for the rich bibliography).

Since the presentation of the evidence is the main purpose of the volume, it fully accomplishes the mission of the archaeologist, according to Carl Nylander, the main person responsible for the excavation of San Giovenale:

> “Every archaeologist knows that an excavation means not only increase of knowledge but also destruction of historical evidence. Thus it is the excavator’s inescapable obligation to save and to transmit that evidence in a new shape as fully and faithfully as ever possible.” (21)

**Arne Furumark** (geboren am [26\. September](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/26._September "26. September") [1903](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/1903 "1903"); gestorben am [6\. Oktober](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/6._Oktober "6. Oktober") [1982](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982 "1982")) war ein [schwedischer](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schweden "Schweden") [Klassischer Archäologe](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klassische_Arch%C3%A4ologie "Klassische Archäologie").

Furumark war Spezialist für Kunst und Keramik der [späten ägäischen Bronzezeit](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sp%C3%A4thelladikum "Späthelladikum"). Sein Hauptwerk zur Chronologie [mykenischer Keramik](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mykenische_Keramik "Mykenische Keramik") erschien 1941 in zwei Bänden. Er strukturierte hierbei das Keramikmaterial unter formalen Gesichtspunkten nach Gefäßtypen. Gerechtfertigt schien ihm diese Methode, weil er dem menschlichen Geist und menschlicher Kultur ein großes Beharrungsvermögen unterstellte, unter dessen Einfluss sich Veränderung nur schrittweise bemerkbar mache. Das Werk ist immer noch ein Standardwerk zur mykenischen Keramik und die von Furumark definierten Typen von Furumark 1 bis 333 werden immer noch international bei der Beschreibung [minoischer](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoische_Keramik "Minoische Keramik") und mykenischer Keramik benutzt.

Nach dem [Zweiten Weltkrieg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zweiter_Weltkrieg "Zweiter Weltkrieg") setzte er in seinem Buch _Det Äldsa Italien_ mit neuen Forschungsansätzen zur [Vorgeschichte](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urgeschichte "Urgeschichte") Italiens neue Maßstäbe. In den Jahren 1947 und 1948 führte er Ausgrabungen im [zyprischen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zypern "Zypern") [Sinda](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinda_/(Zypern/) "Sinda (Zypern)") durch, deren Ergebnisse 2003 von Charles M. Adelman veröffentlicht wurden. 1950 erschien sein umfangreicher Artikel _The Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550-1400 B.C._ in den _Opuscula Archaeologica_. 1952 wurde er Professor für Archäologie an der [Universität Uppsala](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A4t_Uppsala "Universität Uppsala"). Als einer der ersten nutzte Furumark die erfolgreiche Entzifferung der [Linearschrift B](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linearschrift_B "Linearschrift B") durch [Michael Ventris](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris") für seine Forschungen. In den Jahren 1956/1957 war er neben seiner Professur in Uppsala Direktor des [Svenska institutet i Athen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svenska_institutet_i_Athen "Svenska institutet i Athen"), der schwedischen archäologischen Schule in [Athen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athen "Athen"). 1962–1963 führte er weitere Ausgrabungen in Zypern durch[\[1\]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-1). 1970 wurde er emeritiert.

**Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark** (26 September 1903 – 8 October 1982) was a Swedish[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAccorinti2014p._323,_n._3-2) archaeologist who specialised in the ceramics of [Mycenaean Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece "Mycenaean Greece"). His three-volume work _The Mycenaean Pottery_ established a categorisation and chronology of the ceramics of the [Late Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age "Late Bronze Age") on the Greek mainland. A 1943 review credited him with doing "for [Mycenaean pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_pottery "Mycenaean pottery") what [Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humfry_Payne "Humfry Payne") did for Corinthian and [Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beazley "John Beazley") for Attic wares",[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaniel1943252-3) and subsequent scholars have considered the work a standard reference, though it received criticism for an over-rigid approach and for prioritising stylistic analysis at the expense of information about objects' archaeological contexts.

Furumark was born in the Norwegian capital of [Kristiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") (now Oslo).[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-Union-1) After an unhappy childhood, in which he initially seemed set to follow his father into the paper business, he entered [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University") in Sweden in 1925 to study the humanities, and became a pupil of the archaeologist [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"). He obtained his doctorate, with a thesis on the decoration of Mycenaean ceramics, in 1939, and became an associate professor at Uppsala in the same year. He led excavations at [Sinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinta,_Cyprus "Sinta, Cyprus") on Cyprus, the first Swedish archaeological work on the island since the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), between 1947 and 1948, and became a professor at Uppsala in 1952. He remained there until his retirement in 1970, and served a year's term as director of the [Swedish Institute at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_at_Athens "Swedish Institute at Athens"), a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957. He also conducted excavations at [San Giovenale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giovenale "San Giovenale") in Italy between 1962 and 1963, and published on the Mycenaean settlement of the island of [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes").

Although an early sceptic of the idea that the [Linear B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B "Linear B") script was used to write Greek, Furumark corresponded with [Michael Ventris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris"), who deciphered it in 1953, and was one of the first archaeologists to use his conclusion that its language was indeed Greek. Furumark's work on ceramics helped to establish the distinctive nature of mainland Greek ("Helladic") ceramics in relation to Cretan ("[Minoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_civilization "Minoan civilization")") wares, and highlighted the ways in which both cultural groups influenced each other to varying extents over time. In doing so, he helped to overturn the narrative of [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans") that Minoan Crete had dominated mainland Greece throughout the Late Bronze Age. He also established continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following [Protogeometric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protogeometric_style "Protogeometric style"), and thereby that narratives which argued for the complete overturning of Greek culture at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the [Dorian invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_invasion "Dorian invasion"), were incorrect.

Josef Arne Gerdt Furumark was born on 26 September 1903,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4) in the Norwegian capital of [Kristiania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo") (now Oslo),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-5)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-Union-1) where his father worked as a businessman in the paper industry.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198334-7) He suffered from a skin condition throughout his life, which left him shy and socially isolated.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198338-8) Family life during his early years was unhappy; Furumark initially attended business school in Norway and worked in his father's offices in Oslo and in London, where at the age of nineteen he visited the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum"). He later said that this visit encouraged him to change his studies to archaeology. In 1925, he entered Sweden's [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University"), where he studied a wide [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities") curriculum including classical archaeology, philosophy and theology. He eventually came to study there under the Mycenaean archaeologist [Axel W. Persson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axel_W._Persson "Axel W. Persson"),[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198334-7) under whom he took part in excavations in Greece.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9)

Furumark received his doctorate, with a dissertation on the subject of [Mycenaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece "Mycenaean Greece") ceramic decoration, in 1939. In the same year, he was made an associate professor at Uppsala.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) In 1941, he published _The Mycenaean Pottery: Analysis and Classification_ and _The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery,_[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) a two-volume study which analysed, categorised and dated Late Bronze Age ceramics from the mainland of Greece according to their shapes and decorative motifs.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) He had begun writing a third volume, _Mycenaean Pottery: A History,_ by 1941, but abandoned the project by 1944.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas201814-12) He published _Det äldsta Italien_, a handbook of Italian archaeology, in 1947, which became widely cited: he planned, but never published, an edition in English.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197630-13)

Between 1947 and 1948, Furumark excavated at [Sinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinta,_Cyprus "Sinta, Cyprus") on Cyprus.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) Swedish archaeologists had excavated widely on the island before the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), but Furumark's was the first Swedish project there after 1945.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStyrenius19948%E2%80%9312-14) The excavation was conducted in two campaigns; the first from 22 December 1947 to 22 January 1948, and the second from 25 March to 7 May 1948.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurumark200363-15) [Carl-Gustaf Styrenius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl-Gustaf_Styrenius "Carl-Gustaf Styrenius") later credited Furumark's excavations with expanding scholarly knowledge of migration from Greece to Cyprus at the end of the Bronze Age.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStyrenius199412-16) The project uncovered a [Late Cypriot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Cypriot "Late Cypriot") (c. 1300 – c. 1200 BCE) settlement with [Cyclopean walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopean_masonry "Cyclopean masonry"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEG%C3%B6ransson2012419-17) though only excavated a small fraction of its total area of around 46,500 square metres (11.5 acres).[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIacovou200710-18) In 1948, during a visit to the Bronze Age site of [Hala Sultan Tekke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hala_Sultan_Tekke_/(archaeological_site/) "Hala Sultan Tekke (archaeological site)") on the island, he noticed a large [pithos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithos "Pithos") in a field, which prompted new excavations around it.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%85str%C3%B6m1978232-19)

In 1950, Furumark argued, on the basis of the ceramics of Minoan Crete, that the idea of the Cretan site of [Knossos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knossos "Knossos") being ruled by Greek-speakers in the Late Minoan II period (c. 1490 – c. 1430 BCE) was "untenable":[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-20) the fact of mainland rule over Crete in this period was established two years later by [the discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipherment_of_Linear_B "Decipherment of Linear B") by [Michael Ventris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ventris "Michael Ventris") that the [Linear B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_B "Linear B") tablets made there at this time were written in a form of Greek.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990314-21) Furumark had maintained a correspondence with Ventris since 1951;[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHedlund200310-22) after Ventris proposed his decipherment, Furumark worked with [Gudmund Björck](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gudmund_Bj%C3%B6rck&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gudmund Björck (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudmund_Bj%C3%B6rck "sv:Gudmund Björck")), the professor of Greek at Uppsala, to check its accuracy. The two wrote to Ventris in October 1952 to give their verdict that he was correct.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHedlund200311-23)[\[b\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-25) Furumark was one of the first archaeologists to use his decipherment in his own work.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-ArtHistDict-26)[\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-28) Also in 1950, he argued that Mycenaean settlers had arrived on the island of [Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes "Rhodes") around the turn of the Late Helladic IIB and IIIA periods (that is, c. 1400 BCE), that they lived peacefully alongside the pre-existing population, who used [Minoan pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_pottery "Minoan pottery"), and were allowed to live in existing houses. Mario Benzi, in 1988, called this idea "astonishing", and suggested that the Mycenaean incomers more probably subjugated the inhabitants by force.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBenzi198859-29)

Furumark became Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at [Uppsala University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uppsala_University "Uppsala University") in 1952,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476Medwid2000112-30) succeeding Persson.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%85str%C3%B6m20037-31) In the early years of his professorship, he was involved in reorganising the university's collection of antiquities,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) and created a small museum in two of the university's rooms.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) He served as director of the [Swedish Institute at Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_at_Athens "Swedish Institute at Athens"), a research centre for classical archaeology, between 1956 and 1957.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAccorinti2014p._323,_n._3-2) Among his students at Uppsala were [Margareta Lindgren](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Margareta_Lindgren&action=edit&redlink=1 "Margareta Lindgren (page does not exist)"), who worked on Linear B,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENoschEnegren2017xxviii-33) and [Gisela Walberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gisela_Walberg&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gisela Walberg (page does not exist)"), who extended his work on Mycenaean ceramics to those of [Middle Minoan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Minoan "Middle Minoan") Crete,[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHood1978375-34) as well as [Sture Brunnsåker](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sture_Brunns%C3%A5ker&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sture Brunnsåker (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sture_Brunns%C3%A5ker "sv:Sture Brunnsåker")) and [Carl Nylander](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carl_Nylander&action=edit&redlink=1 "Carl Nylander (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Nylander "sv:Carl Nylander")).[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) His own academic work during his professorship, in contrast to his previous studies of Mycenaean and Italian archaeology, focused on the ancient Aegean scripts.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197630%E2%80%9331-35) In 1956, he gave a lecture in Berlin in which he attempted to decipher the [Linear A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_A "Linear A") tablets uncovered at the site of [Hagia Triada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Triada "Hagia Triada") on Crete,[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacKendrick1981120-36) using the methods applied by Ventris to Linear B,[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBraidwoodMason195859-37) and posited that Linear A had similarities with the Anatolian [Indo-European language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages") of [Luwian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luwian_language "Luwian language").[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacKendrick1981120-36)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-39) He was appointed a member of the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") in 1958.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPohl1958412-40) Between 1962 and 1963, he excavated at [San Giovenale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Giovenale "San Giovenale") in Italy,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) continuing excavations begun there in the 1950s by the [Swedish Institute in Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Institute_in_Rome "Swedish Institute in Rome").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarlsson200622-41) After recovering from a period of serious illness in the late 1960s,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTENylander198335-9) he retired from his professorship in 1970,[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476Medwid2000112-30) and was succeeded by his former student Sture Brunnsåker.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrunnsaker197631-32) He died on 8 October 1982 in Uppsala.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4)

Contributions to archaeology
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arne_Furumark&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Contributions to archaeology")\]

Johannes Siapkas, in 2022, identified Furumark as part of a Swedish tradition, traceable back to the work of [Erik Hedén](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Erik_Hed%C3%A9n&action=edit&redlink=1 "Erik Hedén (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_Hed%C3%A9n "sv:Erik Hedén")) at the turn of the twentieth century, to distinguish the academic treatment of the ancient world from the popular understanding of it, and to prioritise scientific objectivity in its reconstruction.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas2022114-42) A 1943 review of _The Mycenaean Pottery_ credited him with doing "for Mycenaean pottery what [Payne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humfry_Payne "Humfry Payne") did for Corinthian and [Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Beazley "John Beazley") for Attic wares";[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaniel1943252-3) Siapkas compared his work with that of [Johann Joachim Winckelmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Joachim_Winckelmann "Johann Joachim Winckelmann") on ancient sculpture.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43)

_The Mycenaean Pottery_ was the first complete survey of its subject published in book form,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) and became the established point of departure for subsequent studies.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43) Furumark's approach developed from that of German stylistic analysis, known as _Strukturforschung_ ('Structural Research'), first practised in the 1920s by archaeologists such as [Friedrich Matz](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Friedrich_Matz_\(born_1890\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Friedrich Matz (born 1890) (page does not exist)") ([de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Matz_der_J%C3%BCngere "de:Friedrich Matz der Jüngere")).[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-45) However, Furumark rejected the association made in _Strukturforschung_, under the influence of [Nazi racial theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_racial_theories "Nazi racial theories"), between cultural styles and biological races.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas201815-46) As well as ceramic vessels, he named and categorised the terracotta figurines known as [psi, phi, and tau types](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psi,_phi_and_tau_type_figurine "Psi, phi and tau type figurine").[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench1971103-47) The archaeologist [Robin Hägg](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Robin_H%C3%A4gg&action=edit&redlink=1 "Robin Hägg (page does not exist)") ([sv](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_H%C3%A4gg_/(arkeolog/) "sv:Robin Hägg (arkeolog)")) described the books as Furumark's "_magnum opus_ ... \[and\] ever since the standard work on this topic";[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEH%C3%A4gg1996476-10) Linda Medwid called them "the definitive reference on the subject" in 2000.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) Although the [absolute dates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_dating "Absolute dating") of Furumark's chronology have generally been revised, the categories and reference he assigned to particular shapes and motifs remain conventional vocabulary within the field.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011258-49)

Furumark's contemporary [Alan Wace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Wace "Alan Wace") criticised him for what he called "excessive [pigeonholing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonholing "Pigeonholing")" of ceramic styles, and for ignoring information about the archaeological contexts in which finds were unearthed; the latter criticism was also articulated by Wace's collaborator [Carl Blegen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Blegen "Carl Blegen").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESiapkas20187-43) [Susan Sherratt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Sherratt "Susan Sherratt"), in 2021, criticised Furumark's approach as "essentially stylistically based and unrealistically over-analytical", particularly by contrast with that of [Lisa French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_French "Elizabeth French"), who worked on Mycenaean pottery in the second half of the twentieth century.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2021-50) [Gerald Cadogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gerald_Cadogan_\(archaeologist\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gerald Cadogan (archaeologist) (page does not exist)") described Furumark's approach as _[dirigiste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirigiste "Dirigiste")_ for what he considered its excessive devotion to ordered categorisation.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTECadogan2003353-51)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-53) Sherratt elsewhere criticised Furumark's system for lumping together variations of shape and motif into single categories, on the basis of what he considered to be evolutionary relationships between them.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011258-49) She also disagreed with his treatment of individual motifs and shapes in isolation, rather than as part of coherent decorative schemes.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTESherratt2011259-54)

### Influence on Minoan and Mycenaean studies

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arne_Furumark&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Influence on Minoan and Mycenaean studies")\]

[![Image 5: Tall, wide-necked vessel decorated with a simple geometric drawing of a chariot.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene%2C_1300-1250_BC%2C_AM_of_Nafplio%2C_202188.jpg/250px-Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene%2C_1300-1250_BC%2C_AM_of_Nafplio%2C_202188.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amphoroid_krater_with_chariot_scene,_1300-1250_BC,_AM_of_Nafplio,_202188.jpg)

Mycenaean [krater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krater "Krater") from the Late Helladic IIIC period, as defined by Furumark

[![Image 6: Vessel decorated with simple geometric drawings of horses.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg/250px-Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Horses_manger_Louvre_A513.jpg)

Furumark argued that the ceramics of the [Mycenaean civilisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_civilisation "Mycenaean civilisation") of mainland Greece were a development of pre-Mycenaean mainland forms, with influence from contemporary Minoan Crete.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000112-4) This aligned with the view set forth by Wace and Blegen in 1918, that the civilisation of mainland Greece had been broadly continuous and indigenous throughout the Bronze Age. This view, known as the "Helladic Heresy" ("Helladic" meaning "native to mainland Greece"),[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaceBlegen1918118%E2%80%93119Galanakis2007241-55) was itself an extension of the archaeological theory of [Christos Tsountas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christos_Tsountas "Christos Tsountas"), who argued for the continuity of Greek culture from prehistory to the modern period.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPliatsika2020292-56) Furumark established the sub-periods of the [Helladic chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helladic_chronology "Helladic chronology") based on the stages of development of pottery styles, which became the standard [relative chronology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relative_dating "Relative dating") system used in studies of the Mycenaean period.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11)

Furumark's findings contradicted the idea of [Arthur Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Evans "Arthur Evans"), who had named Minoan civilisation in the early 20th century, that Mycenaean civilisation had developed from that of Crete.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113Galanakis2007240-57) Furumark concluded that the level of Minoan influence in mainland ceramics changed over time, with an overall balance roughly even between Cretan- and indigenous-derived vessel shapes, a high level of Cretan influence in the Late Helladic IIIA period (c. 1400 – c. 1300 BCE), and a dominant mainland influence in the following Late Helladic IIIIB period (c. 1300 – c. 1180 BCE).[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-58) He therefore rejected both the term "Late Minoan", used for mainland pottery of the Late Bronze Age by Evans and [Duncan Mackenzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Mackenzie "Duncan Mackenzie"),[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) and Wace and Blegen's "Helladic", which he considered to imply that developments on the mainland were isolated from the wider Aegean. Since Furumark's work, the terms "Helladic" and "Mycenaean" have been considered equivalent,[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) though his belief that "Helladic" did not adequately encompass the influence of Crete and the other Aegean islands has generally been rejected by other scholars.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11)

Medwid called _The Mycenaean Pottery_ "a final refutation" of Evans's view that Mycenaean Greece had been subordinate to Minoan Crete, referencing Furumark's demonstration of the continuity of Mycenaean pottery as well as that certain Mycenaean forms, such as the [kylix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kylix "Kylix"), were adopted on Crete.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48) Following the 1938 work of Mogens B. Mackeprang,[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-59) Furumark included two styles of pottery, found by Wace at Mycenae and labelled by him the Granary Style and the Close Style, in his categorisation of the Late Helladic IIIC period (c. 1180 – c. 1050 BCE).[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-60) He identified a trend in the later part of the period towards simple geometric designs,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcDonaldThomas1990300-11) establishing continuity between Mycenaean pottery and that of the following [Protogeometric period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protogeometric_style "Protogeometric style"), and thereby that narratives which argued for complete cultural collapse or replacement at the end of the Bronze Age, such as that of the [Dorian invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_invasion "Dorian invasion"), were incorrect.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Furumark#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMedwid2000113-48)

10.content:
Furumark’s excavations at the Late Bronze Age fortified town of Sinda, some 20 miles east of Nicosia, were conducted more than 50 years ago. Despite lack of publication and the relatively small area uncovered, the site has since played an important role in discussions of the 12th century B.C. in Cyprus. A brief summary report appeared in the _American Journal of Archaeology_ in 1948, and a longer account appeared in Swedish in 1952. These and a more substantial unpublished report written by Furumark in 1951 formed the basis of Adelman’s volume. Collaboration between Adelman and Furumark began as long ago as 1977, but the project remained unfinished on the latter’s death in 1982. The current volume was completed in 1998 but was subject to further delays before its final publication with a summary and conclusions by Paul Åström in 2003.

Adelman’s preface is both a moving tribute to Furumark and a candid account of the many difficulties faced during this long period of gestation. These included torn plans, plans and sections without indication of strata, uncatalogued and fading negatives, incomplete or nonexistent artifact descriptions, missing architectural documentation, and incomprehensible field notes. These problems were compounded by the destruction of the site by local villagers in 1951 and the loss of finds housed in the Famagusta Museum during the Turkish invasion of 1974. There are lessons here for all field archaeologists.

A great deal, of course, has changed since the excavations at Sinda. Furumark’s ceramic terminology in particular is out of date, and his chronology and historical interpretation of the site have been repeatedly challenged. While some ceramic categories are updated in brackets (e.g., Quasi-Mycenaean Linear Ware \[= Painted Wheel-Made III\]), for the most part Adelman’s text and the extensive find catalogues maintain the original terminology. Points of departure between Furumark’s account of the excavations and the final report are, however, clearly defined, and Adelman’s own stratigraphic interpretations, rendered necessary in particular in the description of the South Area, are presented with due warning regarding their accuracy. For the most part the text reads smoothly, in line with Adelman’s stated desire to present the site as much as possible “in the style and with the feeling of Furumark.”

Part 1 of the volume begins with a description of the excavations. These were conducted in three areas (Northwest Area, Gate Area, South Area). While some pre- and post-Late Bronze Age remains were found, the three main periods of occupation (Sinda I–III) were dated by Furumark to Late Cypriot IIC(2), IIIA(1), and IIIA(2). Both Sinda I and Sinda II ended in episodes of destruction. These were attributed by Furumark, respectively, to the arrival of Greek settlers (ca. 1230) and the Sea Peoples (ca. 1190), with Sinda III representing a partial reoccupation prior to final abandonment in ca. 1150 B.C. The Gate Area produced remains of a city gate with wheel tracks, a gate house, and a tower or bastion. Of note is a substantial deposit of votive stone sculpture of Cypro-Archaic and Cypro-Classical date, laid in the late fourth century B.C. as filling for a road that passed through the ruined gateway. In the South Area, where greater soil depth provided better preservation, an area of housing was found. The process of excavation is well illustrated by text photographs. Sections and plans are included as inserts in a pocket in the back cover, and synoptic tables provide a schematic presentation of strata and find distribution.

In part 2 Adelman provides a brief treatment of the history and significance of the site. He notes the need for a reassessment of the Sinda material in light of recent ceramic studies but unfortunately makes no attempt to do so. Addressing the question of who built Sinda and why, it is suggested that the settlement controlled the only crossing of the Pedieos River on the copper route from Idalion and Athienou to Enkomi, perhaps exacting tolls from travelers and traders. Adelman suggests that the site was surrounded by a double wall, with the remains excavated by Furumark belonging to the inner system. Difficulties in distinguishing catastrophe material from pre-floor fills are noted but not considered overly problematic, and life at Sinda is conventionally described as lively and prosperous, the inhabitants engaged in agriculture, food production, craft activities, and bull worship.

It is left, indeed, to Paul Åström to take up the challenge of reviewing Sinda and its two destruction levels in the light of more recent discoveries and within the highly contested context of the history and chronology of Late Cypriot III. Åström suggests a lowering of the dates proposed by Furumark in line with a lowering of the end of Mycenaean IIIB. Thus, Period I, which produced Mycenaean IIIB pottery, ends ca. 1190/1180 B.C., Period II in ca. 1150/1140, and Period III in ca. 1110/1100 B.C. This lowered chronology raises the possibility that the first destruction at Sinda was brought about by the Sea Peoples and not, as Furumark proposed, by Greek settlers. Åström’s own view is that both destructions were caused by pirates and adventurers consisting of Mycenaeans and groups from other areas, or possibly by conflict between Cypriots themselves. Whatever the case, this final publication of Sinda will no doubt give rise to renewed debate about events in Cyprus in the 12th century and, as Åström notes, further fuel discussion of the radical low chronology proposed by some scholars for Palestine via oft-noted links between Sinda Mycenaean IIIC1b and Philistine pottery.

Part III contains extensive find catalogues with summary indexes and a listing of all classes of material with accompanying high-quality black-and-white illustrations and line drawings. While some items (e.g., a stamp seal) are discussed in detail, most appear only as catalogue entries with typological attribution and some comparanda. Contextual data and Furumark’s views on ceramic style and chronology are reported where relevant. Sherd counts by ware and stratigraphic context and other distributional and statistical data are further presented in part IV and an appendix. The animal remains are reported by Gejvall, translated from a Swedish original of 1951.

Adelman is to be commended for taking on an extremely difficult task and achieving a fine result for which scholars of the Cypriot Bronze Age have cause to be grateful. The volume lacks a contemporary reading of the ceramic evidence and were it not for the important contribution by Åström would also be missing a serious analysis of the historical significance of Sinda. It is clear, however, that Adelman’s main objective was to retrieve and present the basic stratigraphic, architectural, and artifactual data, and he has done this in full and painstaking detail. In making the primary data available to other scholars, he has acquitted the primary obligation of the original excavator and ably fulfilled the demands and responsibilities of a collaborative task for which few of us would have had either the courage or patience.

Jennifer M. Webb  
Archaeology Program  
La Trobe University  
Bundoora, Victoria 3083  
Australia

Swedish excavations at Sinda, Cyprus. Excavations conducted by Arne Furumark 1947–1948
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[Arne Furumark](https://ecsi.se/tag/arne-furumark/) & [Charles M. Adelman](https://ecsi.se/tag/charles-m-adelman/), with contributions by [Paul Åström](https://ecsi.se/tag/paul-astrom/), [Nils-Gustaf Gejwall](https://ecsi.se/tag/nils-gustaf-gejwall/) & [Hans Henning von der Osten](https://ecsi.se/tag/hans-henning-von-der-osten/)

Abstract
--------

When Arne Furumark was entrusted with writing the Late Bronze Age summary volume for the Swedish Cyprus Expedition, he realized that a habitation site was needed in order to clarify problems associated with the last phases of that period. As neither the French nor the Cypriot excavations at Enkomi had yet been published he decided to find his own site: he scouted several, but settled on Sinda because recent illicit digging there had thrown up sherds of a sort never before seen on the island, namely Mycenaean IIIC1b. He conducted two short excavation seasons but the control excavation he planned was aborted when he received notice from Cypriote authorities that there was large scale destruction of the site.

Although there is evidence of earlier and later habitation at Sinda, the most important is the Late Bronze Age fortified town (probably built along the copper trading route), with its three phases: Sinda I, II and III. Sinda I, which saw the building of the defense system and had material culture including local Cypriot wares as well as examples of Mycenaean IIIB, suffered major destruction. Sinda II followed: structures were repaired and built, and were accompanied by a rich material culture including Mycenaean IIIC1a and great quantities of locally produced, early IIIC1b materials. A second catastrophe brought an end to that town. Sinda III followed, a poorer town, but with examples of locally produced, developed IIIC1b wares of the Close Style.

Furumark’s interpretation that the two destructions were brought about first by Greek settlers and then by Sea Peoples has been challenged by more recent archaeological evidence which lowers the date of Mycenaean IIIB. Paul Åström, in his summary suggests a reasonable alternative, that pirates and adventurers (Mycenaean and groups from other areas) were responsible for the destructions.

Swedish excavations at Sinda
============================

The village of Sinda is in the district of Famagusta, in northern Cyprus, about 20 km from Nicosia. Close to the village is a necropolis with chamber tombs dated to the Late Bronze Age, as well as tombs from Hellenistic and Roman times. There are also the remains of a Bronze Age settlement in the vicinity. In 1947, Arne Furumark, Professor of Classical Antiquity at Uppsala University, conducted an initial investigation, which led him to decide that further archaeological fieldwork at the site could be very interesting. An excavation directed by Furumark began in December 1947 and was followed by a second field season in the spring of 1948. In 1949, after permission had been granted by the Cypriot authorities, many of the finds were brought to Sweden.

Many of the objects from the collection are shown in Gustavianum's exhibitions. Parts of the collection are also available to researchers and students at The historical collections at EBC, Center for Evolutionary Biology.

![Image 2: A man sitting next to an excavation.](https://www.uu.se/images/18.30f49183187eaded81b1a2c0/1684765128591/Arne%20Furumark%201948.jpg)Arne Furumark during excavations at Sinda in 1948.

Want to know more about the collection?
---------------------------------------

As a private individual, you can access the objects in our collections in various ways. Look out for [our events](https://www.uu.se/en/gustavianum/exhibitions), visit the [Gustavianum's various exhibitions](https://www.uu.se/en/gustavianum/exhibitions) or search for the objects on the [digital platform Alvin](http://www.alvin-portal.org/alvin/home.jsf?dswid=-7547). If you have specific questions, you can [contact our antiquarians](https://www.uu.se/en/gustavianum/contact) for each collection.

**Description:**

**Mycenaean Pottery**

Introduction by J.R. Green

The Mycenaeans were finally proved to be Greeks by the decipherment of Linear B in 1952. They had arrived in what we now call Greece about the turn of the second millennium bc and quickly developed a distinctive style of which one aspect is its pottery. The development of the palace culture seems to have occurred around the time of the transition from what is termed Middle to Late Helladic, in the 16th century, and there is evidence of a successively more centralised political system until its collapse around 1200 BC.

Decorated Late Helladic pottery is finely made with well-worked clay produced on a fast wheel. The applied paint is typically a glossy red-brown, often characterised by neat brushwork. The extent of Mycenaean external contacts is demonstrated by the wide distribution of the pottery in Cyprus, the Near East and Egypt (which has provided the best evidence for its chronology), and then in the West in South Italy, Sicily, the Aeolian Islands, Etruria, Sardinia, and even as far as Spain. Indeed there seems to have been local production in South Italy, as there clearly was in Cyprus.

The first serious study of Mycenaean pottery was that by Adolf Furtwängler and Georg Loeschcke, _Mykenische Vasen: vorhellenische Thongefässe aus dem Gebiete des Mittelmeeres_ (Berlin 1886). The next major step was the classificatory work of A. Furumark, _The Mycenean Pottery. Analysis and Classification_ (Stockholm 1941) and _The Chronology of Mycenean Pottery_ (Stockholm 1941), and they have only recently begun to fall out of general use. During the 1960s E.B. French published a series of vital articles in _BSA_ establishing a finer sequence based on stratified deposits from Mycenae, and many other regional studies have appeared since. The main items are listed in the bibliographies of the two useful handbooks by P.A. Mountjoy, _Mycenaean Decorated Pottery. A Guide to Identification_ (Studies in Mediterranean Archaeology vol. 73, Göteborg 1986) and _Mycenaean Pottery: An Introduction_ (Oxford University Committee for Archaeology Monograph no. 36, Oxford 1993).

Those interested in issues of trade and contact should consult C. Zerner, P. Zerner and J. Winder (eds.), _Wace and Blegen. Pottery as Evidence for Trade in the Aegean Bronze Age, 1939-1989. Proceedings of the International Conference, Athens 1989_ (Amsterdam 1993). On chronological issues, P. Warren and V. Hankey, _Aegean Bronze Age Chronology_ (Bristol 1989) is vital.

See also the Mycenaean terracotta figurines, under ‘Terracottas’.

**Full Name:** Furumark, Arne

**Gender:** male

**Date Born:** 1903

**Date Died:** 1982

**Home Country/ies:** Sweden

**Subject Area(s):** Aegean, ancient, archaeology, bronzes (visual works), and metalwork (visual works)

### Overview

Archaeologist, specialist in late Aegean Bronze Age art; professor at Uppsala University 1952-70. Furumark’s major work, _The Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery_ appeared in 1941. It remains the standard work on the subject. After World War II, his innovative research into the prehistory of Italy was published in 1947 as _Detäldsa Italien_. He excavated Cyprus 1947-48 (at Sinda). In 1950 his “Settlement at Ialysos and Aegean History c. 1550-1400 BC,” was published. He was director of the Swedish Institute in Athens, 1956-57. Furumark returned to Cypriot excavations 1962-63.Furumark employed Ventri’s desciphering of Linear B for his own work; he was one of the first. _Chronology of Mycenaean Pottery_ made use of formal shape typologies to date the pottery. “Furumark” 1 through 333 is used internationally in the description of Mycenean and Minoan pottery.
